stages.title: Advantages of price controls
stages.sub: After this you can explain why governments use maximum and minimum prices to improve fairness and correct under- or over-consumption.

steps.q: Bread is a basic essential. If its price is left to the free market and rises sharply, who struggles most to afford it: rich households or poor households?
steps.hint: Think about who has the least spare income to absorb a price rise.

steps.hint: Look at the maximum price diagram: the price falls, so who benefits from paying less?

steps.q: A vaccine benefits not just the person who takes it but everyone around them who avoids catching the disease. Does the free market price account for those extra benefits to others?
steps.right: No, it ignores those extra benefits
steps.wrong: Yes, it fully accounts for them
steps.hint: Think about who the buyer considers when deciding how much to pay: just themselves, or everyone affected?
steps.pre: A good like this, whose benefits to society exceed the benefits to the buyer alone, is a

steps.q: Cigarettes harm not just the smoker but also people nearby through passive smoke. Does the free market price the smoker pays include this extra harm to others?
steps.right: No, it leaves out that harm
steps.wrong: Yes, it fully includes that harm
steps.hint: Think about what the smoker pays for: just their own cigarettes, or also the harm to others?

steps.q: A government sets a maximum price for the vaccine below equilibrium, so more people buy it, moving consumption closer to what's best for society. Does this pull consumption towards or away from the social optimum?

steps.q: A government sets a minimum price for cigarettes above equilibrium, raising the price smokers pay closer to the true cost including harm to others. Does this make the price smokers pay reflect more, or less, of the harm to third parties?
steps.right: More of the harm to third parties
steps.wrong: Less of the harm to third parties
